Error type impact
Sorted by "Edge lost" — total R this mistake has cost you vs. your clean-trade baseline, worst first. "Win rate"/"Avg RR" count a trade toward every tag it carries (so they can add up to more than your total trades); "Solo WR (n)" isolates trades where this was the only tagged error, to check whether the mistake is bad on its own or only in combination — watch the n, small samples aren't conclusive.
Issue evolution over time
The top chart plots the % of that period's trades each error type was tagged on, so you can see which mistakes you're growing out of and which are creeping back in; the bottom chart shows the same trend in raw trade counts. Dashed green is your clean-trade rate for comparison. Click a name in the legend to isolate that line in both charts (hide the rest); click it again to bring everyone back.

Checklist Item Breakdown by Setup Rating
Which checklist items get skipped most — and whether skipping them actually costs you. Pick a setup rating to see what's dragging trades into it; "All rated trades" pools everything with a checklist logged.
Most missed checklist items
Checklist items by weightiWeight is the point value each item is worth toward your setup-rating score, set per item in the Checklist editor. A trade's score is the sum of the weights of every item checked on it, and that score is what the tiers (A+, A, B+...) are thresholded against — so a heavier item swings the rating more than a lighter one.
Sorted by weight, heaviest first — not affected by the rating filter above, since weight is a fixed property of the item, not something computed per trade. The heaviest few items usually decide most of your score, so this is where to look if you want to know what actually moves your rating.
Item-by-item breakdown
Sorted by miss rate, worst first. "WR impact" compares win rate on trades where the item was checked vs. where it wasn't — a wide gap means this item is actually predictive, not just a box to tick.
Rating-blocking items
Across every trade that fell short of a higher tier, these are the single unchecked items whose weight alone would have closed the gap. Ignores the dropdown above — it's about every under-rated trade. Fix these first for the fastest lift in your average setup rating.

Edge Statistics
Built from every filtered trade's R-multiple (actual result ÷ initial risk). Expectancy is your average R per trade — the number that determines whether you make money over a large sample. Significance testing asks: could this expectancy plausibly be zero (no real edge) and you're just seeing noise? Small samples make that hard to rule out, so treat anything under ~30 R-tracked trades as a hint, not a verdict.
Equity curve (cumulative R)
Running total of R across trades in chronological order. A real edge should trend up and to the right more often than not, even with drawdowns along the way.
Rolling expectancy (20-trade average R)
Average R of each trade and its previous 19, plotted through time. Watch whether it stays above the dashed zero line — an edge that's drifting toward zero may be decaying (market conditions changing, discipline slipping, etc.).
R-multiple distribution
How this is calculated
·
Core statistics
ExpectancyYour average R per trade — the number that decides if you're profitable long-run.
Mean R across R-tracked trades in the current filter.
Std. deviationHow much your R-multiples swing from trade to trade.
Sample standard deviation of R (n−1).
SQN / t-statVan Tharp's System Quality Number — a quality score for the edge.
Expectancy ÷ (std. dev ÷ √n) — Van Tharp's System Quality Number; also the test statistic for "is mean R different from zero". Rule of thumb: <1.0 poor, 1.0–1.6 below average, 1.7–2.5 average, 2.6–3.9 good, 4.0–6.9 excellent, 7.0+ exceptional (and worth double-checking for errors).
p-valueOdds your edge is really zero and you're just seeing noise. Below 0.05 = significant.
One-tailed probability of seeing an expectancy this far from zero, in the observed direction, if the true long-run edge were exactly zero (exact Student's t-distribution, n−1 degrees of freedom — not a normal approximation, which would understate this at small n). Below 0.05 is the conventional "statistically significant" bar.
95% CIThe range your true long-run expectancy plausibly falls in.
Expectancy ± (t-critical value for n−1 df) × standard error. This assumes your R's are roughly symmetric around the mean.
Bootstrap 95% CIThe same range, estimated a sturdier way that doesn't assume a shape. Needs 10+ trades.
Resamples your actual R-multiples with replacement 2,000 times, takes the mean of each resample, and reads the 2.5th–97.5th percentile off that distribution. It makes no assumption about the shape of your results, unlike the t-based CI above — which matters because real trade outcomes are usually skewed (many small results, a few big ones). Needs 10+ R-tracked trades to compute. If the two intervals broadly agree, that's independent confirmation the t-based CI is trustworthy. If they disagree — the bootstrap dips to zero when the t-interval doesn't, or it's meaningfully wider — treat that as a sign the mean is being carried by a handful of skewed outcomes rather than a stable, repeatable process; this tool will downgrade an otherwise-green verdict when that happens.
Period coveredHow much calendar time and how frequently you've traded.
Calendar days between the first and last R-tracked trade in the filter, and trades/week over that span.
Costs & profitability
Fee drag / Net expectancyAll stats above are net of your estimated real trading costs, not raw price-move R.
The verdict and all stats above are computed on R-multiples net of estimated trading costs (spread, commission, overnight/swap, margin interest, short-borrow fee, SEC/FINRA regulatory fees), using your current per-asset-type fee settings (Manage Assets & Pairs) applied to each trade's qty/entry price/duration/direction. This matters because the raw R-multiple logged per trade is pure price-move vs. stop-distance and never includes costs — a gross edge can be statistically real and still be flat or a net loser once real costs are counted, especially for small-target or high-frequency setups. Two caveats: it uses your currently configured fees applied retroactively, so it won't reflect a broker or fee change partway through your history; and trades missing asset type, quantity, or risk-dollar data are left at gross R (treated as zero-fee) since no cost can be estimated for them — check the "Fee drag" card's coverage count if this matters to you.
Breakeven win rateThe win rate you'd need just to break even, given your win/loss sizes.
100 ÷ (1 + payoff ratio) — the win rate you'd need just to break even given your current avg win/loss size.
Robustness checks
Best/top-3 trade share of RChecks whether your edge is really just one or two lucky trades.
Your single best (or best 3) R-tracked trade's result, as a % of the total R summed across the whole filtered sample — plus what average R looks like with that trade (or 3) removed. A high share, or a mean that turns flat/negative once removed, means the result is leaning on one or two lucky trades rather than a repeatable process. This check runs even on a "significant" green verdict and will downgrade it if the edge doesn't hold without the outlier.
Split-sample checkCompares your older trades vs. recent ones — is the edge still showing up? Needs 20+ trades.
Your R-tracked trades, in chronological order, split down the middle — expectancy on the older half vs. the more recent half. The t-test and bootstrap both ask "is the full-sample average unlikely to be zero"; this asks a different question: does the second half still look like the first, or has whatever produced the edge already stopped showing up in more recent trades. Needs 20+ R-tracked trades (10+ per half) to compute. A full-sample edge that's positive only because of a hot early stretch — recent half flat or negative — will downgrade an otherwise-green verdict, the same way the outlier and bootstrap checks do.
Runs test (streakiness)Checks if wins/losses are independent, or clustering from tilt/revenge trading. Needs 20+ trades.
A Wald-Wolfowitz test on the chronological win/loss sequence (breakevens excluded) — counts how many "runs" (streaks of the same outcome) actually occurred vs. how many independent, randomly-ordered trades would be expected to produce, then checks whether that gap is bigger than chance explains. This is different from every other check above: those ask whether the average R is real; this asks whether the trades behind that average were actually independent, which the t-test, CI, and bootstrap all assume. Needs 20+ decisive (non-breakeven) trades with at least 5 wins and 5 losses to compute. Too few runs means wins and losses are clustering — a sign of tilt, revenge trading after a loss, or a market regime that came and went — and will downgrade an otherwise-green verdict, since it means the significance test above is more confident than the data supports. Too many runs (excessive alternating) is flagged too, but doesn't move the verdict — it's unusual rather than a known risk pattern.
"Statistically significant edge" (green) requires all of: 30+ R-tracked trades, at least 30 days between the first and last of them, and the 95% CI staying above zero. A p-value below 0.05 alone is not enough — a handful of trades can pass that test by luck, and trades clustered in a short window only ever test one market regime. Below either floor, the verdict caps at amber even if the math already looks significant.
This is a statistical estimate from historical data, not a guarantee — it assumes trades are independent and R is roughly stable over time, which is rarely perfectly true in live markets. It also can't correct for filter-shopping: slicing by enough pairs, sessions, or directions will eventually turn up a subset that looks "significant" by chance alone, so treat a good result on a narrow filter with extra skepticism, not less. Use it as one input, not the whole decision.

JSON Backup & Restore
Export JSON
Downloads 4 separate files — trade data (trades, images, sessions & settings), config (strategies, checklist, asset pairs, theme, AI & Cloudinary selections), FX (USD/CAD conversions) and watchlists — the exact same data a GitHub Manual Backup pushes, just downloaded instead of pushed. Alerts are not included.
Restore JSON
Select one or more of the JSON files above (trade data, config, FX, watchlists — any combination); each is detected automatically. Deletes your existing trades, images and sessions first, then loads only what's in the selected file(s) — a true restore, just like GitHub's "Restore latest". Config/FX/Watchlist files always fully overwrite the matching settings. All-or-nothing — if any selected file is invalid, nothing is touched. Also syncs the actual GitHub data files (not the bkp/ backup folder) if GitHub is configured.
Merge JSON
Select one or more of the JSON files above (trade data, config, FX, watchlists — any combination); each is detected automatically. Keeps your existing data and merges in trades, images, sessions, config, FX and watchlists from the selected file(s) — duplicate trades are skipped, nothing existing is deleted. Config/FX/Watchlist files still fully overwrite the matching settings. All-or-nothing — if any selected file is invalid, nothing is touched. Also syncs the actual GitHub data files (not the bkp/ backup folder) if GitHub is configured.
GitHub Not configured
Repository Setup
Create a private GitHub repo (e.g. my-trading-journal), then generate a Personal Access Token at github.com/settings/tokens with repo scope. Your token is stored only in this browser.
Push to GitHub
Manually push your full journal — trades, images, sessions, settings, watchlists, config (strategies, checklist, assets & pairs), price alerts and FX conversions — to your GitHub repo right now.
Pull from GitHub
Restore your full journal — trades, images, sessions, settings, watchlists, config, price alerts and FX conversions — from GitHub. Use this on a new browser or device. Existing data is merged (no duplicates).
Last sync
Never synced yet. Auto-sync runs after every trade save once configured.
Backup & Snapshots
Manual Backup
Saves a timestamped trades snapshot to bkp/trades/ and overwrites the single config backup at bkp/config_backup.json with all current settings (strategies, checklist, pairs, columns, theme, defaults), plus the single FX backup at bkp/fx_backup.json with your USD/CAD conversions.
Restore / Merge Latest Trade Backup
Uses the most recent snapshot in bkp/trades/. To restore your config (strategies/checklist/pairs), use the Snapshots list below. Restore deletes your current trades, images and sessions first, then loads only what's in the snapshot. Merge keeps your current data and adds in the snapshot's trades, images, sessions and settings — duplicate trades are skipped.
Automatic Weekly Backup Off
Runs the exact same backup as Save manual backup above — automatically, once a week, on the day and time you set.
Needs GitHub configured above. This app has no server, so the schedule is only checked while the app is open in a tab (on load, and every few minutes after) — it won't fire while your browser is fully closed. If the scheduled moment passes while you're away, it catches up once, the next time you open the app.
Trade, Config, FX & Watchlist Backups
bkp/trades/ · bkp/config_backup.json · bkp/fx_backup.json · bkp/watchlist_backup.json
Trade Backups — timestamped snapshots in bkp/trades/. Created automatically before session deletes and clear-all, or manually. Multiple snapshots kept so you can roll back to any point.

Config Backup — a single file at bkp/config_backup.json storing strategies, checklist, and asset pairs. Auto-updated whenever you change any of those, and on Manual Backup. Only one backup kept — always the latest.

FX Backup — a single file at bkp/fx_backup.json storing your USD/CAD conversions from the FX Tracker page. Updated on Manual Backup. Only one backup kept — always the latest.

Watchlist Backup — a single file at bkp/watchlist_backup.json storing all your watchlists and categories. Updated on Manual Backup. Only one backup kept — always the latest.
Deploy to GitHub Pages
⚠ Use a separate public repo for Pages. GitHub Pages requires a public repo on free accounts. Your data repo must stay private — it contains your full trade history. Create a second repo (e.g. trading-journal-app) that holds only this HTML file. Your GitHub sync credentials still point at your private data repo — nothing changes there.
Steps to deploy:
  1. Create a new public repo on GitHub (e.g. trading-journal-app) — not your data repo
  2. Add this index.html file to your repo root
  3. Download the workflow file below and commit it to .github/workflows/deploy.yml
  4. In that repo's Settings → Pages, set source to GitHub Actions
  5. Push — your journal will be live at https://<user>.github.io/trading-journal-app
  6. On any new device, open the URL, go to Backup & Restore, enter your private data repo credentials and hit Pull
Cloudinary — Image Hosting Not configured
When configured, screenshots are uploaded to Cloudinary (free tier: 25 GB) instead of being stored as base64. Your tj_data.json stays tiny — only image URLs are saved, not the image data itself.

Sign up free at cloudinary.com, then go to Settings → Upload → Upload presets and create an unsigned preset. Copy your Cloud Name from the dashboard.

⚠ Required for screenshot deletion: In your upload preset settings, under Upload Control, set Return delete token to Yes. Without this, removed screenshots will not be deleted from Cloudinary.
How it works: When you paste or drop a screenshot, it's uploaded instantly to Cloudinary. The image URL is stored in your trade. Your GitHub backup stays lean — no base64 blobs. Existing trades with base64 images continue to work normally.

Cloudflare Worker — Deploy Guide Reference
No CLI needed. The worker is deployed entirely through the Cloudflare dashboard — copy, paste, save. A free account is all you need. All config (tokens, keys, alerts) is stored in KV and pushed from this page via Save and Sync.
Adding Cloud Monitor to a vanilla HTML copy?
Download the patch file — it has the three blocks (CSS, HTML, JS) you need to paste in, with exact search anchors for each insertion point.
1. CSS → paste before the </style> that follows .pa-updated-ago
2. HTML → paste before <!-- /page-price-alerts -->
3. JS → paste before the final </script> at end of file
  1. Create a free Cloudflare account at dash.cloudflare.com if you don't have one.
  2. Go to Workers & Pages → Overview, click Create → Create Worker. Name it (e.g. journup-price-alerts) and click Deploy.
  3. Click Edit code, delete the placeholder, paste the full price-alerts-worker.js contents (download below), then click Deploy.
  4. Create a KV namespace. Workers & Pages → KV → Create namespace. Name it JOURNUP_KV.
  5. Bind the KV namespace. Worker → Settings → Bindings → Add → KV namespace. Variable name: JOURNUP_KV (exact). Select the namespace. Save.
  6. (Optional) Worker Secret. Settings → Bindings → Add → Secret. Name: WORKER_SECRET. Enter the same value in the Worker Secret field above.
  7. Set cron trigger. Settings → Triggers → Cron Triggers → Add. */1 * * * * = every minute, */5 * * * * = every 5 min.
  8. Copy your worker URL, paste it into Cloudflare Worker URL above, then click Save and Sync.
⚠ KV binding variable name must be exactly JOURNUP_KV — a typo causes a runtime error.
Worker endpoints
POST /config — push tokens, keys & settings
GET  /config — read config from KV
POST /alerts — sync active alerts array
GET  /alerts — read alerts from KV
GET  /trigger_log — last 200 fired alert entries
POST /poll — manually trigger a price check now
GET  /status — worker health & alert counts
GET  /debug?sym=BTCUSDT — test all price providers for a symbol
GET  /price?symbol=EURUSD — live price fetch (no KV, direct from provider)
